Title: [Epidemiological characteristics of three local epidemics of COVID-19 in Guangzhou].
Authors: Zhao WH, Ma Y, Wang H, Li K, Dong H, Liu WH, Liu YY, Jiang SQ, Luo L, Yang ZC.
Citation: Zhonghua Liu Xing Bing Xue Za Zhi. 2021 Dec 10;42(12):2088-2095. doi: 10.3760/cma.j.cn112338-20210728-00592.
Journal/Book: Zhonghua liu xing bing xue za zhi = Zhonghua liuxingbingxue zazhi
Keywords: [MeSH] Adult; [MeSH] COVID-19; [MeSH] China; [MeSH] Epidemics; [MeSH] Female; [MeSH] Humans; [MeSH] Male; [MeSH] SARS-CoV-2
Abstract: Objective: To understand the epidemiological characteristics of three local COVID-19 epidemics in Guangzhou and provide reference for optimizing strategies and measures of COVID-19 prevention and control. Methods: The data of local COVID-19 cases in Guangzhou reported as of June 18, 2021 were collected from National Notifiable Disease Report System of China. The software Excel 2019 and SPSS 22.0 were applied for data cleaning and statistical analysis. Results: A total of 726 COVID-19 cases were reported in the three local epidemics in Guangzhou. In the epidemic associated with the outbreak of COVID-19 in Hubei province, 366 cases were reported. Most cases were female (51.6%, 189/366), aged 18-65 years (81.4%, 298/366), jobless/unemployed (32.2%, 118/366) and retired persons (20.2%,74/366). The initial symptoms of most cases were fever (71.6%, 250/349) and cough (60.7%, 212/349). In the epidemic associated with the imported COVID-19 cases from Africa, 207 cases were reported. Most cases were aged 18-40 years (72.9%, 151/207), male (69.6%, 144/207), and engaged in commercial services (62.3%,129/207). The initial symptoms of most cases were no obvious discomfort (55.6%, 15/27) and cough (37.0%, 10/27). In the epidemic associated with Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2, 153 cases were reported, in which women accounted for 58.8% (90/153), most cases were over 41 years old (64.7%,99/153), and retired persons accounted for the highest proportion (32.0%,49/153). The initial symptoms of most cases were cough (32.9%, 48/146) and no obvious discomfort (28.1%, 41/146). The household secondary attack rates of the three local epidemics were 11.2%, 5.7% and 11.5%, respectively. The median (P25, P75) of incubation periods were 6.5 (4.0,10.8) d, 4.0 (2.5, 6.0) d and 4.0 (3.0,5.0) d. The serial intervals median (P25, P75) were 4.0 (3.0, 8.0) d, 4.0 (2.5, 6.0) d and 3.0 (2.0,5.0) d. There were significant differences in gender, age, occupation, initial symptoms, household secondary attack rate and incubation period among the three local COVID-19 epidemics (all P<0.05). In the proportion of the case finding way, passive detection in patient treatment were mainly 44.3%(162/366) in the epidemic associated with the outbreak of COVID-19 in Hubei province,but active community case screening [58.5% (121/207) and 27.5% (24/153)] and close contact management in imported case were mostly [33.3% (69/207) and 67.3% (103/153)] in the epidemic associated with the imported COVID-19 cases from Africa and with Delta variant of SARS-CoV-2, respectively. Conclusions: Due to the different sources of infection, strain types and prevention and control strategies, the epidemiological characteristics of the three local COVID-19 epidemics in Guangzhou differed in demographics, clinical symptoms, transmission routes and case finding, which suggested that it is necessary to improve the key population and common symptom monitoring in the routine prevention and control of COVID-19 to prevent the reemerge of the epidemic.
overall_justification: This is a human, real-world, original epidemiologic study of COVID-19 outbreaks in Guangzhou that explicitly reports serial interval estimates and includes a Delta-associated epidemic. Its relevance is moderated because the paper is broader than variant-specific transmission-interval analysis and only one of the three epidemics is explicitly variant-linked.
disease_justification: The abstract concerns COVID-19/SARS-CoV-2 and explicitly includes one epidemic associated with the Delta variant. However, the paper is not solely focused on variant-specific transmission parameters, as it compares three epidemics with mixed sources/strain contexts.
population_justification: The study analyzes reported human COVID-19 cases in Guangzhou, with demographic and clinical characteristics of 726 cases. Humans are clearly the population of interest.
location_justification: The study is set in a real-world geographic context: three local epidemics in Guangzhou, China, using surveillance data. This is explicit field-based epidemiology.
evidence_justification: The abstract reports primary analysis of case data collected from the National Notifiable Disease Report System of China. It presents original empirical results, not a review or commentary.
parameter_justification: The abstract explicitly reports serial interval medians for the three epidemics, including the Delta-associated epidemic (3.0 [2.0, 5.0] days). However, it reports serial interval rather than generation interval/time, and the variant-specific estimate is only one part of a broader descriptive comparison.

Title: Proportion of Pre-Symptomatic Transmission Events Associated with COVID-19 in South Korea.
Keywords: COVID-19; Delta variant; Korea; SARS-CoV-2; expanded testing; incubation period; mathematical; pre-symptomatic; serial interval; statistical
Abstract: Pre-symptomatic transmission potentially reduces the effectiveness of symptom-onset-based containment and control strategies for the coronavirus disease (COVID-19). Despite evidence from multiple settings, the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission varies among countries. To estimate the extent of pre-symptomatic transmission in South Korea, we used individual-level COVID-19 case records from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency and Central Disease Control Headquarters. We inferred the probability of symptom onset per day since infection based on the density distribution of the incubation period to stratify the serial interval distribution in Period 1 (20 January-10 February 2020) and Period 2 (25 July-4 December 2021), without and with expanded testing or implementation of social distancing strategies, respectively. Assuming both no correlation as well as positive and negative correlations between the incubation period and the serial interval, we estimated the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission in South Korea as 43.5% (accounting for correlation, range: 9.9-45.4%) and 60.0% (56.2-64.1%) without and with expanded testing, respectively, during the Delta variant's predominance. This study highlights the importance of considering pre-symptomatic transmission for COVID-19 containment and mitigation strategies because pre-symptomatic transmission may play a key role in the epidemiology of COVID-19.
overall_justification: The full text confirms strong relevance to SARS-CoV-2, humans, and real-world field epidemiology, and it contains an original Delta-predominant serial interval estimate derived from transmission pairs. However, this is not primarily a serial-interval/generation-time paper: the main outcome is pre-symptomatic transmission proportion, with serial interval used as an input, and generation interval/time is not directly estimated. Overall, the paper is meaningfully related but only moderately well confirmed for the review’s specific target parameter focus.
disease_justification: The full text explicitly studies SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 and repeatedly frames Period 2 as occurring during 'the Delta variant’s predominance' in South Korea, with Period 2 selected because Delta accounted for more than 50% of local cases after 25 July 2021.
population_justification: This is a human population study using individual-level confirmed COVID-19 case records from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, including 279,059 reported cases and 29,009 transmission pairs in South Korea.
location_justification: The analysis is set in a real-world geographic context—South Korea—with national surveillance and contact-tracing data and clearly defined calendar periods tied to local epidemic conditions and interventions.
evidence_justification: The study performs a primary empirical analysis using original Korean case records and estimates a serial interval for Period 2 from 29,009 transmission pairs, although it also relies on previously published incubation-period estimates and earlier-period parameter values.
parameter_justification: The paper does report a variant-era serial interval estimate in the full text and Table 1 for the Delta-predominant period (mean 3.15-3.2 days, 95% CI 3.10-3.20), and it discusses approximating generation time from serial interval. However, the central aim is estimating the proportion of pre-symptomatic transmission, not directly estimating/comparing serial interval or generation interval/time across variants, and no direct generation-interval estimate is reported.

Title: Serial interval distribution of SARS-CoV-2 infection in Brazil.
Authors: Carlos A Prete, Lewis Buss, Amy Dighe, Victor Bertollo Porto, Darlan da Silva Candido, Fábio Ghilardi, Oliver G Pybus, Wanderson K de Oliveira, Júlio H R Croda, Ester C Sabino, Nuno Rodrigues Faria, Christl A Donnelly, Vítor H Nascimento
Keywords: COVID-19; basic reproduction number; epidemiologic measurements; generation interval; serial interval
overall_justification: The full text strongly confirms a real-world human primary study that directly estimates serial interval from Brazilian transmission pairs. However, this is an early-pandemic SARS-CoV-2 paper with no variant, lineage, Delta, Omicron, or other variant-specific analysis, so it does not truly satisfy the variant-focused review question despite reporting the target parameter in general.
disease_justification: The full text is clearly about SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19, but it studies early 2020 transmission in Brazil and does not mention any variant, lineage, sublineage, or variant comparison anywhere in the article.
population_justification: This is a human epidemiologic study using 65 confirmed infector-infectee pairs from Brazil provided by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, based on national case notification data.
location_justification: The study is set in a real-world geographic context in Brazil, using national surveillance data from cases notified between 25 February and 19 March.
evidence_justification: The paper reports original empirical analysis of 65 infector-infectee pairs and directly estimates the serial interval distribution from observed symptom-onset dates, with model fitting and supplementary sensitivity analyses.
parameter_justification: The target parameter is explicitly central: the paper estimates the serial interval ('mean serial interval of 2.97 days', median 3 days, SD 3.29) and discusses generation interval in keywords/background. However, it does not provide variant-specific serial interval, generation interval, or generation time estimates, which is required for this review question.
